analysis.one_liner: Hands federal oil and gas permitting on public land to the states, exempting it from federal environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any state that already regulates oil and gas on its own land declare that it will take over federal leasing and permitting for energy development on federal land within its borders. Once a state took over, its decisions would no longer count as federal actions, so they would be exempt from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the federal Administrative Procedure Act. Royalties would still go to the same federal accounts as before, but states could keep permit application fees and would no longer wait on federal agencies.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies seeking to drill on federal land would get faster permits and no federal environmental review of their projects. States with energy industries would gain control over development decisions on land owned by all Americans, and they could keep application fees. Renewable and other energy developers on federal land could also benefit from state-controlled permitting.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land

how_it_helps.text: A state with an established leasing, permitting, and regulatory program can declare it will take over federal responsibilities for leasing, permitting, and regulating oil, natural gas, and other forms of energy development on federal land in that state, and then do so in place of the federal government.

State actions to lease, permit, or regulate energy development are exempted from the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act, removing federal environmental and legal review from those projects.

The bill's findings argue federal permitting was slow, taking 197 days to process drilling applications in 2013, and that federal land leased for oil and gas fell from 131 million acres in 1984 to 36 million acres in 2013.

States could collect and retain application processing fees, while royalties and other revenues must still be collected at the same levels and deposited in the same federal accounts as if the leases had been federally issued.

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which owns federal land in common, would bear the cost of projects approved without environmental review, without protection for endangered species, and without preservation review for historic sites. Communities near drilling sites would face decisions made entirely under state law with no federal check. Treasury collections from royalties are preserved, so taxpayers would not directly lose revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through lost environmental review

drawbacks.text: Exempting state-approved energy projects from the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act would remove the main federal checks on drilling on land owned by all Americans, leaving protection of those lands to whichever state hosts the project.

State regulators who already oversee the oil and gas industry in their state would both regulate and promote development on federal land within their borders, with no independent federal review of their decisions.

Even supporters' own findings concede the bill's purpose is to overcome reduced federal leasing and long permitting times, meaning its effect is to open more federal land to development faster than the existing federal process would allow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades faster, state-run permitting for the loss of national environmental, endangered species, and historic preservation review on federal land. The revenue side is neutral to the Treasury. The main beneficiaries are energy developers; the main risk falls on the public lands and wildlife that belong to everyone, which only the removed federal review would have defended.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up or sent it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator James Inhofe introduced the bill on February 12, 2015, with Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The bill received no further action of any kind after the referral, and it died at the end of the 114th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who value environmental review of drilling on federal public land are better off because the bill never advanced; oil and gas companies are no better off than before, since federal permitting rules remained unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public and its environmental protections

for.name: Sen. James M. Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eight colleagues to cosponsor it on introduction day.

for.name: 10 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican and no Democrat signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Senate Republicans out of 54; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land
industries.note: The bill would give these companies a state-run permitting path with no National Environmental Policy Act review, no Endangered Species Act consultation, and no Administrative Procedure Act challenges, on land owned by all Americans. Their gain comes directly from the removal of review that protects the public's land.

industries.industry: Renewable and other energy developers on federal land
industries.note: The bill covers 'other forms of energy' on federal land, so wind, solar, and geothermal developers could also use the state permitting path. The same removal of federal environmental review would apply to their projects.

industries.industry: Federal land and wildlife management agencies
industries.note: Interior, Agriculture, and Energy would lose their leasing, permitting, and regulatory authority over energy development on state-declared federal land, along with the environmental review roles those agencies perform on behalf of the public.
